title: The Memorare
hook: remember, O most gracious Virgin, that never was it known

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salve Regina: the night song of ordinary days, honest about the valley of tears. Your line was hail, holy queen. Did you give one honest answer, tear and hope both? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

Never. Asking for something usually comes wrapped in hedges. Sorry to bother you. No pressure. Only if you have time. Here's a prayer that does the opposite. It doesn't open by asking. It opens by reminding. Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, it begins, that never was it known that anyone who fled to your protection, asked for your help, or sought your prayers, was left without help. Never was it known. That's a bold thing to say out loud, especially when you're the one in need. It sounds less like a petition and more like a child tugging a sleeve and saying, you always come. Today's word is the prayer's first word.
screen: `MOST ASKING COMES WITH HEDGES.` → `THIS PRAYER BEGINS BY REMINDING.` → `NEVER WAS IT KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Memorare is Latin for remember, and it gives the prayer its name. Start there. The one praying asks Mary to remember her own record. It's the way you'd speak to a friend who has always come through: you know what you're like. The prayer stands on memory. Then the bold line. Never was it known. That isn't a survey or a statistic. It's a statement of trust, the kind people make about those they love. The one who prays it is saying: in the stories we've been handed, she didn't turn anyone away. Where does that trust come from? Some Catholics point to a wedding at Cana. In John's Gospel, the wine runs out at a wedding, and Mary notices and tells her son. In the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." Then she turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." She sees a need, and she brings it to Jesus. The Memorare asks her to do that again. Then the posture. The prayer goes on: inspired with this confidence, I fly to you, and before you I stand, sinful and sorrowful. Confidence and humility in the same breath: I know you'll help, and I know I don't deserve it. It ends by asking the mother of the Word made flesh not to despise these words, but to hear and answer. Who wrote it? Tradition credits Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, and others trace its spread to a later French priest, also named Bernard. Nobody needs to settle it to pray it. The prayer itself only asks you to remember.
screen: `MEMORARE: REMEMBER.` · `NEVER WAS IT KNOWN: A STATEMENT OF TRUST.` · `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `CONFIDENT AND SORROWFUL AT ONCE.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Memorare. Settle, and breathe. Bring one need to mind, the one you'd hedge about if you were asking a person. Name it plainly, without the sorry-to-bother-you. Then, if you pray, pray the Memorare once, slowly, from remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, to hear and answer me, and set your need inside it the way you'd set a note inside an envelope. If you don't pray, remember instead: one time someone noticed what you needed before you asked, and came. Let that memory sit with you for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Memorare. Latin for remember: the prayer that opens by reminding Mary that never was it known that anyone who came to her was left without help. Today's word.
Your line: never was it known. Today, be someone's Cana: notice one need nobody has named, and do something about it before you're asked. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Memorare on their own, in hard moments and as a regular devotion, and some pray it in a short run of repetitions when they bring an urgent need to Mary.

fork.setup: you're a guest at a wedding in Cana, and you notice the wine has run out. what do you do?
options: say nothing. it's not your party.
go to Jesus: they have no wine.
slip out before it gets awkward.
fork.reveal: Mary goes to her son with "they have no wine," then tells the servants, "whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye" (John 2:3–5). the Memorare asks her to notice again.

original.note: Latin: remember, the prayer's first word and its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer asking for a favor.
what it means: a prayer that opens by reminding Mary of her record: never was it known that anyone was left without help.
what a scholar hears: memorare, remember; trust grounded in Cana (John 2:3–5); and authorship credited by tradition to Bernard of Clairvaux, its spread to a later Bernard.
recall: a line from the Song of Songs

sources.quoted: Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.

notes: The Memorare is paraphrased and partly recited without quotation marks, close to the traditional English; its translation is not on the validator's public-domain list. Confirm wording of the parts used ('Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known that anyone who fled to thy protection, implored thy help, or sought thy intercession was left unaided'; 'Inspired by this confidence, I fly unto thee... before thee I stand, sinful and sorrowful'; 'O Mother of the Word Incarnate, despise not my petitions, but in thy mercy hear and answer me').

Authorship: traditionally attributed to Bernard of Clairvaux; often traced in its spread to Fr. Claude Bernard (17th century). Stated as 'tradition credits... others trace its spread to a later French priest, also named Bernard'. Confirm.
'Some Catholics point to a wedding at Cana' is the script's framing of a common Catholic reading; consider 'some Catholics'.
howItsDone mentions praying it in repeated runs (the 'flying novena'); described without a number. Confirm.
Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of John 2:3 ('And the wine failing, the mother of Jesus saith to him: They have no wine.') and 2:5.

Editor pass: Cana retold as the text has it (Mary notices and tells her son), cutting 'before anyone asks her' and 'a need nobody has named', which John 2 doesn't say; 'Catholics who pray it are saying... in all the stories' narrowed to the one who prays it.
